The judgments are **BENIGN** for all three supplied files. The decisions follow independent recovery of the code and its effects; earlier review notes and scanner findings were investigation leads. Suspicious concealment is retained independently of these verdicts.

| Original / identity | Hostile before → after | Suspicious before → after |
|---|---:|---:|
| `123d1e44ac3e` / Afterglow 11.0.0 | 0 → 0 | 0 → 0 |
| `649f710e32a6` / Rifaien self-submission client | 0 → 0 | 0 → 0 |
| `cc6ccb7ca50b` / Lumin game SDK | 0 → 0 | 1 → 1 |

All nine analyzed archive members remain at zero hostile and zero suspicious. Each of the three fetched jsDelivr copies of the Lumin SDK remains at **0 hostile / 1 suspicious**; the registry metadata remains at zero for both. The three URLs serve the same supplied SDK bytes. [review.json](review.json) records every member/dependency, exact trait changes, raw classifier output, hashes and limitations. All original classifier routes remain class 0 (BENIGN), agreeing with these judgments; a large `prob` value is not substituted for the emitted class. The model warns that its v18 feature schema predates the engine's expected v21.

Afterglow has an empty npm entrypoint, no installation hook, and a browser application. Its root HTML redirects to a frame-based game portal. The SVG fetches the package's HTML and writes it into a frame. The main distribution includes Arctic's proxy/browser and games UI, endpoint fallback, user accounts/settings, optional tab disguises, and local chat history. The AI handlers transmit chat and explicitly selected attachments. Screen capture starts through the visible screenshare button and `getDisplayMedia`; “Ask about screen” captures a JPEG and routes it through the same media sender. The callbacks do not expose an operating-system command channel. The referenced Arcade SDK was fetched and read: it retrieves a game catalog and game HTML, renders search/categories, and opens selected games. The referenced Arctic document was also fetched; the wrapper removes its advertising and analytics scripts before insertion.

The Lumin SDK's name, `fonts.min.js`, conceals its actual role. Bounded QuickJS evaluation recovered five fallback origins, `/api/v1/boot`, the request token, and 35,326 bytecode words. Forager fetched that boot response with provenance. Its first field is compiled with `(0,Function)(i[0])()`; the returned VM interpreter consumes the bytecode and a 10,680-character string pool. The offline control-flow disassembler follows functions, jumps, exception destinations and fallthrough edges, recovering 9,602 instructions. At words 6286–6399 it publishes `Lumin.init`, search, game/category methods, player controls and events. The surrounding functions implement catalog rendering, iframe playback, worker loading, endpoint probes/cache, and Google Analytics.

The referenced `/v1/lumin.worker.js` was fetched as well. Its embedded interpreter is Base64/XOR encoded. Decoder-only evaluation and static traversal recovered another 3,097 instructions. The dispatch at words 8742–9179 handles initialization, game search/catalog/category requests, game URL probes and fallback rotation. It creates its own session through POST `/api/v1/session`, reads that response's `session_id`, and uses it as `X-Session` for game APIs. These are application sessions, not harvested browser credentials. The fetched worker and both extracted interpreters were scanned and inspected. The recovered behavior matches the [publisher's game-SDK documentation](https://docs.luminsdk.com/). Runtime source generation and obscured code remain relevant signals even with a benign implementation.

Rifaien's standard UPX unpacking fails its checksum. Unicorn ran only the decompressor and E8/E9 repair, stopping at `0x428716`, before import resolution or application execution. The reconstruction restores the imports at their image-relative addresses and preserves the recovered exports. CRT startup reaches main at `0x4013a0`. Main reads its complete own executable with `GetModuleFileNameA` and CRT file I/O. It finds `[[UNIQUE]]`, selects NODE1 through NODE7, changes sixteen bytes, writes a randomly named executable, and supplies that same path to libcurl's multipart form. The fields are `file[]`, `node`, and `submit`; the URL is `http://wecan.hasthe.technology/upload`. It deletes the generated file and repeats after 30 seconds. The response is not interpreted as code or commands.

The endpoint and numbered-node schema fit the historical public upload-and-run VM playground, documented in contemporary [participant discussion](https://forum.blockland.us/index.php?topic=264500.210) and the [historical description](https://www.explainxkcd.com/wiki/index.php/350). This positive program-purpose evidence tips BENIGN over unauthorized propagation. Host deployment authorization and current server ownership are unknown. A security engineer should retain the mutation and network-submission findings; a public-testing purpose is not a blanket exclusion.

The appended PE begins at file offset `0x14c8b`, leaving 95,093 bytes. Its `.text` alone requires bytes through offset 105,472 relative to that PE; its resource section requires much more. It is incomplete. Startup, initializers and main expose no extraction, mapping or execution path to it: the trailer is included as data when the whole self-image is copied/uploaded. Its decoder-looking bytes and malicious-family signatures do not establish that the submission client activates another payload.

The likely explanations for the external labels are the portal's filter-bypass/disguise functionality, the SDK's misleading asset name and virtualized remote bootstrap, and Rifaien's continuous self-mutation/submission plus its truncated protected-PE trailer. The data sources' actual labeling rationale is unavailable. These are explanations consistent with the recovered behavior, not proof of the sources' internal reasoning. The AI endpoint returned HTTP 524 after retries; its server-side implementation remains unavailable. Mutable CDN responses and future server behavior are outside the recovered bytes.

The YAML changes retain the supported observations:

- Add a notable custom-alphabet integer decoder. Its AST query binds the input/alphabet/base parameters, indexed character consumption, weighted modulo digit, termination test and emitted integer; it uses no sample identifiers or endpoints.
- Separate Function construction from execution. The generation query now recognizes the comma-expression form. Indirect `eval` and invocation of a constructed Function require the actual callee AST, excluding examples quoted inside another call. Constructed execution also recognizes nested body-producing calls. The suspicious JSON/XOR/storage composite is renamed for runtime evaluation and accepts either actual evaluator; it no longer treats an unused Function as execution.
- Move the numbered-executable printf template from `fs/write/file/target` to `data/format/string`, updating its exact identity consumer. A format string proves no file write. Its matcher, scope, confidence and notable severity are unchanged. Ancestor file-write consumers were inspected; a filename alone must not satisfy their write claim.
- Retain the exact mutation/submission technique, reducing the composite from hostile to suspicious. Mutation and multipart self-submission establish concealment and distribution, but neither unauthorized infection nor remote activation. The native atom and submission capability are unchanged. The valid reconstruction changes from **1 hostile / 1 suspicious** to **0 hostile / 2 suspicious**. The original packed sample remains **0 / 0** because automatic unpacking still fails.

Before the shared corrections, exact and ancestor consumers and relevant positive fixtures were inspected. Forager recovered outside-batch originals `aab86b1c39df…` and `2017070104a4…` with provenance. The uncompressed `aab86…` main is byte-identical to all 834 recovered main bytes in this batch, and its real mutation/submission findings remain, now suspicious. Mutating away the random mutation call or changing the output buffer prevents that technique claim. The retained high-severity findings on three unrelated hostile controls—ghappier's fetched-eval loader, a Base64 HTML loader, and a school-page cloak—are unchanged.

`check.py` passed **25 controls**, including decoder renaming/whitespace, wrong data bindings, quoted/commented code, construction without invocation, actual eval/constructed execution, and the real native positive and near misses. No supported attack capability is lost. The intentional losses are the unsupported execution claim on construction-only code, the filename-as-write implication, and the hostile interpretation of self-submission alone. The original packed file's mutation-loop coverage remains an unpacking limitation; no duplicate or specimen-specific hostile rule was added to conceal that gap.

Reproduce the focused checks with `python3 testdata/triage/afterglow-fonts-rifaien-followup-20261024/check.py --work <scratch>/review-bad --baseline <clean-rule-tree>`. Decoder scripts, disassemblies, raw scans/facts, fetched artifacts and their `.forage.json` files are retained at the scratch path in `review.json`. Reconstructions are analysis artifacts, not original binaries. No sample application, browser payload, child process or self-upload was executed.
